papers.title_in_file: Quantum Boltzmann machine learning of ground-state energies
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proposes a hybrid quantum-classical stochastic-gradient algorithm (QBM-GSE) that uses parameterized thermal states (quantum Boltzmann machines) to approximate ground-state energies, with a quantum gradient estimator and a polynomial sample-complexity proof.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper that runs a hybrid Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (H-HHL) linear-system algorithm on a noisy simulator and on IBMQ 5, 15 and 20 qubit processors for specially constructed gate-based matrices, and compares its runtime at equal fidelity with classical circuit simulation on historical supercomputers.

existing.note: The paper's own benchmark (Fig. 4, Discussion) compares the 20-qubit QPU at 0.04% fidelity with an equal-fidelity Schrodinger-Feynman simulation, and states that present supercomputers Tianhe-1 and Summit surpass the IBMQ QPU; only twentieth-century supercomputers and laptops are slower. The authors also say they compared against the most straightforward simulations, and that tensor networks may solve it in poly-logarithmic time. The advantage claim is narrowed to these conditions.
existing.value: The authors state that their quantum solution of a problem of dimension two to the seventeenth, a record for linear systems on quantum computers, demonstrates algorithmic quantum advantage over classical solutions; their own benchmark compares the IBMQ Johannesburg processor at 0.04% fidelity with an equal-fidelity straightforward Schrodinger-Feynman simulation, and finds twentieth-century supercomputers and modern laptops slower but present supercomputers Tianhe-1 and Summit faster than the QPU.
existing.anchor: Conclusion, p.6; Discussion and Fig. 4 caption, p.5
quotes: The implemented quantum solution of a 217-dimensional problem, which is a record for a linear system solution on quantum computers, demonstrates algorithmic quantum advantage over classical solutions.
